knowledge:ch18:s18.3-18-3-succession-pat.content_summary: Pathway: Sale to Third Party (Strategic Buyer); Description: Negotiate sale to competitor, customer, supplier, or other strategic acquirer seeking operational synergies; Tax Treatment: Stock sale: capital gains treatment preferred by seller; Asset sale: ordinary income on recaptured depreciation, capital gains on remaining; negotiated; Cash at Close: High—strategic buyers typically pay highest prices (synergy premium) and prefer cash; Control Transfer: Complete; Suitability: Owners wanting maxim…
knowledge:ch18:s18.3-18-3-succession-pat.raw_text:
Pathway: Sale to Third Party (Strategic Buyer); Description: Negotiate sale to competitor, customer, supplier, or other strategic acquirer seeking operational synergies; Tax Treatment: Stock sale: capital gains treatment preferred by seller; Asset sale: ordinary income on recaptured depreciation, capital gains on remaining; negotiated; Cash at Close: High—strategic buyers typically pay highest prices (synergy premium) and prefer cash; Control Transfer: Complete; Suitability: Owners wanting maximum price and clean exit; no family/management buyers available; Key Risks: Employee retention post-sale; earn-out risk; due diligence exposure; integration failure
Pathway: Sale to Private Equity; Description: Sell majority stake to PE fund; retain minority stake and often management role for 3–7 year hold period; second bite of the apple at PE exit; Tax Treatment: Same as third-party sale; rollover equity in new entity may defer gain; Cash at Close: Moderate-High—PE typically uses leverage; seller takes rollover equity risk; Control Transfer: Partial then complete; Suitability: Owners wanting capital liquidity plus growth upside; comfortable with PE culture and reporting requirements; Key Risks: PE governance requirements; rollover equity illiquid; forced exit at PE's timetable; leverage amplifies business risk
Pathway: Management Buyout (MBO); Description: Sell to existing management team; typically financed with combination of management equity, bank debt, seller financing, and possibly PE minority; Tax Treatment: Same as third-party; installment sale treatment for seller note portion; Cash at Close: Low-Moderate—management rarely has cash; seller typically finances significant portion; Control Transfer: Complete (to management); Suitability: Owner with loyal management team ready to lead; owner wants legacy continuation; no family buyers; Key Risks: Management ability to perform without founder; seller financing risk; key man risk post-sale
Pathway: Employee Stock Ownership Plan (ESOP); Description: Create trust to purchase company stock on behalf of employees; seller receives cash/notes; employees accumulate beneficial interest over time; Tax Treatment: C-corp sellers can defer/eliminate capital gains via IRC Sec. 1042 rollover into QRP; S-corp distributions to ESOP are tax-free; significant tax shield; Cash at Close: Moderate—ESOP finances purchase through bank debt and seller financing; not immediate cash; Control Transfer: Gradual—to ESOP trust; board retains management control; Suitability: Owners with loyal workforce; tax-motivated sellers (esp. C-corps); owners wanting legacy continuation; profitable businesses with $2M+ EBITDA; Key Risks: Ongoing ESOP administration costs; employee relations if stock declines; leverage risk; complex compliance (ERISA)

knowledge:ch18:s18.4-18-4-buy-sell-agree.heading: 18.4 Buy-Sell Agreements: Protecting Business Continuity
knowledge:ch18:s18.4-18-4-buy-sell-agree.content_summary: A buy-sell agreement is a legally binding contract among business owners (or between owners and the business entity) that governs what happens to an owner's interest upon triggering events: death, disability, retirement, divorce, bankruptcy, or voluntary sale to outside parties. Without a well-drafted buy-sell agreement, a triggering event can destabilize the business and create devastating financial consequences for all parties.

- Cross-Purchase Agreement: Each owner agrees to purchase the departing owner's interest proportionally. With two owners, each buys the other's interest. - Fixed Price: Set a specific price at execution; update periodically (annually recommended). Risk: price becomes stale between updates; disagreements about when to update; often inadequately updated in practice.

knowledge:ch18:s18.4.2-valuation-in-buy-.raw_text:
How the business is valued at a triggering event is perhaps the most important—and most frequently contested—provision in buy-sell agreements. Three common approaches:
- Fixed Price: Set a specific price at execution; update periodically (annually recommended). Risk: price becomes stale between updates; disagreements about when to update; often inadequately updated in practice.
- Formula Price: Establish a formula (e.g., 5x prior year EBITDA; 1.5x book value). Advantage: self-updating; disadvantage: formula may not reflect true value during industry cycles; EBITDA manipulation risk.
- Appraisal Method: Independent certified valuation at time of triggering event. Most accurate; most expensive; most time-consuming; potential for dispute over selection of appraiser or methodology. Consider requiring three appraisals with median selected.
▌ BUY-SELL FUNDING CRITICAL POINT: Life insurance is the most common funding mechanism for buy-sell agreements triggered by death, providing immediate liquidity exactly when needed—at the moment of a partner's death when business cash flow may be disrupted. The key is matching coverage amounts to current business value and updating policies as the business grows. Underinsured buy-sell agreements are extremely common and can force business sales at fire-sale prices.

knowledge:ch19.heading: Chapter 19: International and Cross-Border Wealth Management
knowledge:ch19.content_summary: Chapter 19: International and Cross-Border Wealth Management
knowledge:ch19.raw_text: Globalization has created an expanding population of clients with international financial complexity: US citizens living abroad, foreign nationals living in the US, clients with foreign assets or businesses, internationally mobile executives, and immigrant entrepreneurs. knowledge:ch19:s19.1.1-the-us-worldwide-.raw_text:
- Citizenship-Based Taxation (CBT): US citizens and permanent residents (Green Card holders) must file US tax returns and pay US taxes on worldwide income regardless of where they reside. This creates compliance obligations for the estimated 9 million Americans living abroad.
- Foreign Tax Credit (FTC): To mitigate double taxation, the US allows a credit for foreign taxes paid on foreign-source income. The credit is limited to the US tax on the foreign income. High-tax countries (UK, Germany) often produce excess credits; low-tax countries create US tax liability.
- Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE): US citizens meeting bona fide residence or physical presence tests can exclude up to $126,500 (2024, indexed annually) in foreign earned income from US taxation. Excludes wages and self-employment income; does not exclude passive income (dividends, interest, capital gains).
- Foreign Housing Exclusion/Deduction: Additional exclusion for housing costs above a base amount; amount varies by location (higher in expensive cities like London, Hong Kong, Singapore).

knowledge:ch19:s19.3.1-covered-expatriat.heading: Covered Expatriate Determination
knowledge:ch19:s19.3.1-covered-expatriat.content_summary:
An expatriating individual is a 'covered expatriate' if they meet any of the following three tests at the time of expatriation:
- Net Worth Test: Net worth of $2 million or more on the date of expatriation.
- Tax Liability Test: Average annual net income tax liability exceeds $201,000 (2024, indexed annually) for the 5 years preceding expatriation.
- Certification Test: Cannot certify (under penalty of perjury) compliance with all US tax obligations for the 5 preceding years.

▌ EXIT TAX PLANNING: Pre-expatriation planning is essential and must begin years before the planned expatriation date. Strategies include: gifting appreciated assets to reduce estate (gifts to US citizen spouses are unlimited; gifts to non-citizen spouses are limited); realizing gains in high-basis years; contributing to IRAs (which receive special treatment); and carefully timing the expatriation date to optimize tax outcomes. Attempting to avoid covered expatriate status requires careful multi-year financial management.

knowledge:ch19:s19.4.1-residency-determi.raw_text:
The US taxes foreign nationals based on their tax residency status—distinct from immigration status:
- Lawful Permanent Resident (Green Card) Test: Green Card holders are US tax residents from the first day of their Green Card and remain residents until the Green Card is officially abandoned or revoked—regardless of how little time they spend in the US.
- Substantial Presence Test: Non-Green Card holders who spend sufficient time in the US become tax residents. The test counts all days in the current year plus 1/3 of days in the prior year plus 1/6 of days two years prior. If the total exceeds 183 days and the person was present at least 31 days in the current year, they are a tax resident.
- Closer Connection Exception: If the substantial presence test is met but the individual has a 'tax home' in a foreign country and a closer connection there, they can avoid US residency for the current year. Must file Form 8840.
- Treaty Tiebreaker: Tax treaties with approximately 60 countries include tiebreaker provisions that may override domestic US residency rules for individuals who qualify as residents of both countries.
paragraphs: The US taxes foreign nationals based on their tax residency status—distinct from immigration status:

knowledge:ch20:s20.1.1-protective-put-po.heading: Protective Put (Portfolio Insurance)
knowledge:ch20:s20.1.1-protective-put-po.content_summary:

knowledge:ch20:s20.1.1-protective-put-po.raw_text:
The most straightforward hedging strategy: purchase put options on an index (S&P 500, Nasdaq) or individual stocks. A put gives the holder the right to sell the underlying at the strike price, providing protection if prices fall below the strike.
Example: Investor holds a $5 million equity portfolio. Purchases put options on SPY (S&P 500 ETF) with strike price 5% below current price, expiring in 12 months. Cost: approximately 2–4% of portfolio ($100,000–$200,000). If market declines 30%, put options gain in value, offsetting approximately 25% of portfolio loss (30% - 5% deductible).
Key considerations: Option premium is a real cost—essentially an insurance premium that expires worthless if the market doesn't decline. Rolling protection annually costs 2–4% per year, meaningfully reducing long-term compounding. Most cost-effective when implied volatility (VIX) is low.
paragraphs: The most straightforward hedging strategy: purchase put options on an index (S&P 500, Nasdaq) or individual stocks. A put gives the holder the right to sell the underlying at the strike price, providing protection if prices fall below the strike.

Example: Investor holds a $5 million equity portfolio. Purchases put options on SPY (S&P 500 ETF) with strike price 5% below current price, expiring in 12 months. Cost: approximately 2–4% of portfolio ($100,000–$200,000). If market declines 30%, put options gain in value, offsetting approximately 25% of portfolio loss (30% - 5% deductible).

Key considerations: Option premium is a real cost—essentially an insurance premium that expires worthless if the market doesn't decline. Rolling protection annually costs 2–4% per year, meaningfully reducing long-term compounding. Most cost-effective when implied volatility (VIX) is low.

knowledge:ch20:s20.1.3-volatility-strate.raw_text:
VIX (CBOE Volatility Index) represents the market's expectation of future 30-day volatility. When markets decline sharply, the VIX typically spikes (the 'fear gauge'). This negative correlation makes volatility exposure a portfolio diversifier.
- Long Volatility via VIX Options: Purchasing VIX call options provides exposure that typically profits during market dislocations when VIX spikes. Cost: significant—options decay rapidly and VIX mean-reverts. Best used as tail risk protection rather than permanent holding.
- Volatility Risk Premium (Short Volatility): Systematically selling volatility (via VIX futures or writing options) harvests the 'volatility risk premium'—the tendency of realized volatility to be lower than implied volatility. Profitable most of the time but experiences severe losses during volatility spikes.
- Dispersion Trading: Sell index volatility while buying single-stock volatility, profiting from the correlation structure of the index. Sophisticated institutional strategy.

knowledge:ch20:s20.2.1-individual-ldi-fr.raw_text:
The LDI approach begins with defining liabilities:
- Essential Liabilities: Non-negotiable spending commitments—basic living expenses, mortgage payments, essential healthcare. These must be funded under all scenarios.
- Important Liabilities: Strongly preferred spending—travel, home renovation, family gifts. Funded under most scenarios but can be reduced if necessary.
- Aspirational Liabilities: Nice-to-have—vacation home, major gift to charity, luxury spending. Funded only from surplus.
Once liabilities are classified, assets are matched to them:
- Liability-Matching Portfolio (LMP): Treasury bonds, TIPS, and immediate annuities matched to essential liability duration. These assets are invested with no expected return premium above the risk-free rate—they exist purely to ensure essential liabilities are funded.
- Return-Seeking Portfolio (RSP): The remaining assets (after LMP funding) are invested in a growth-oriented portfolio (equities, alternatives) to fund aspirational goals and grow wealth.

knowledge:ch20:s20.3-20-3-tail-risk-fund.raw_text:
Certain investment strategies are specifically designed to profit from or protect against extreme market events ('tail risks').
Strategy: Long-Only Tail Risk Funds; How It Works: Purchase cheap out-of-the-money options; hold minimal equities; designed to produce massive returns during crashes (50x–100x option value); Historical Tail Risk Performance: 2020 COVID crash: some funds returned 2,000%+; 2008-2009: strong performance; Normal Environment Performance: Significant negative carry (1–3% drag annually from option decay); designed to lose in normal markets; Typical Allocation: 1–3% of portfolio (small allocation, large crash protection); Key Managers: Universa Investments (Mark Spitznagel), Taleb-related funds
Strategy: Managed Futures (CTAs); How It Works: Trend-following algorithms that go long or short across equity, bond, currency, and commodity futures based on price trends; Historical Tail Risk Performance: 2008: +18% average CTA; 2022: +26% average while stocks fell 18%; 1987: strong; Normal Environment Performance: Flat to slightly negative in trending-up equity markets; performs poorly in choppy, mean-reverting markets; Typical Allocation: 5–15% of portfolio; Key Managers: Man AHL, Winton Group, Campbell, Millburn, Chesapeake
Strategy: Long Volatility (Vol Funds); How It Works: Systematic purchase of options and variance swaps; profits when realized volatility spikes above implied; Historical Tail Risk Performance: 2020 COVID: very strong; 2008: strong; 2011 European crisis: good; Normal Environment Performance: Negative carry of 5–15% annually; designed to lose in low-vol environments; Typical Allocation: 2–5% of portfolio; Key Managers: Capstone, LongTail Alpha, Artemis Capital
Strategy: Risk Parity; How It Works: Allocate risk (not dollars) equally across asset classes; typically results in significant leverage on bond allocation; Historical Tail Risk Performance: 2008-09: less protected than hoped due to leverage unwinding; 2022: significant losses due to bond-equity correlation breakdown; Normal Environment Performance: Strong in environments with diversified asset class performance and stable volatility; Typical Allocation: Can replace traditional 60/40 as core allocation; Key Managers: Bridgewater All Weather, AQR Risk Parity
Strategy: Gold / Precious Metals; How It Works: Store of value that tends to rise during financial crises, inflation, and dollar weakness; Historical Tail Risk Performance: 2008-09: +5% while stocks fell 50%; 2022: flat while stocks fell 18%; 2020: +25%; Normal Environment Performance: Moderate returns; zero yield; inflation-linked over very long periods; Typical Allocation: 3–10% of portfolio; Key Managers: Physical gold, GLD ETF, gold miners (GDX)

knowledge:ch21.heading: Chapter 21: Practice Management for Wealth Advisors
knowledge:ch21.content_summary: Chapter 21: Practice Management for Wealth Advisors
knowledge:ch21.raw_text: Building a successful, durable, and scalable wealth management practice requires skills that go far beyond investment and financial planning expertise. Practice management encompasses client acquisition, retention, team building, operations, technology, and the business of advice itself. Advisors who excel in practice management build enterprises with significant value—firms that can be sold, transitioned to successors, or scaled to serve many more clients with the same or less effort.

knowledge:ch21:s21.1.1-defining-the-idea.raw_text:
The counterintuitive truth of practice management is that defining a narrow, specific ideal client actually accelerates growth by enabling differentiation, referrals, and operational efficiency. Key dimensions of ideal client definition:
- Financial Profile: Net worth range, income level, account size, complexity of financial situation. Advisors specializing in the $1M–$5M segment serve different needs than those serving $10M+ clients.
- Life Stage: Young professionals accumulating wealth, pre-retirees, retirees, business owners, inheritors. Each life stage has distinct planning needs and emotional relationship to money.
- Industry/Occupation: Tech executives with RSUs and ISOs, physicians with student debt and practice ownership, small business owners planning for succession, corporate executives with NQDC plans.
- Values and Priorities: Clients who prioritize sustainable investing, philanthropic planning, family legacy, or financial independence require different conversations and services.
- Geography: Local presence may matter for business owner clients who want face-to-face interaction; national or virtual practices may prefer client demographics that are comfortable with digital relationships.

knowledge:ch22.heading: Chapter 22: Client Communication and Relationship Management
knowledge:ch22.content_summary: Chapter 22: Client Communication and Relationship Management
knowledge:ch22.raw_text: Excellent client communication is the foundation of a durable advisory practice. Research consistently finds that clients who feel their advisor communicates proactively and clearly are dramatically more likely to remain clients, provide referrals, and expand their relationship—regardless of market performance. This chapter addresses communication strategy, challenging conversations, multigenerational relationship management, and the psychology of the client-advisor relationship.

Timing: Tax Season (February–April); Communication Type: Tax Planning Update; Content Focus: Tax documents status; prior year tax implications of portfolio activity; opportunities for current year (Roth conversions, HSA contributions); Format: Email or call; coordinate with client's CPA if relationship exists; Purpose: Position advisor as tax-aware partner; introduce tax planning opportunities

Timing: Year-End (October–December); Communication Type: Year-End Tax Planning; Content Focus: Tax-loss harvesting opportunities; Roth conversion considerations; charitable giving timing; RMD execution if applicable; year-end gifting; Format: Call + written action list; coordination with CPA critical; Purpose: Most actionable planning window; demonstrate tax awareness

knowledge:ch22:s22.2.1-common-difficult-.raw_text:
- Underperformance Discussions: Acknowledge the client's experience of disappointment without being defensive. Provide context (benchmark comparison, market environment). Distinguish between advisor-controlled variables (fees, tax efficiency, risk positioning) and market variables (returns). Reanchor to the long-term plan. Example response: 'I know this quarter was painful to watch—you're absolutely right that the numbers are disappointing. Let me share how your portfolio performed relative to what we'd expect given your allocation, and then talk about whether anything has changed in your situation that should change our approach.'
- Spending vs. Saving Tension: Use objective financial planning software to show the client—not tell them—the impact of their spending on goal achievement probability. Monte Carlo analysis showing 43% probability of meeting retirement goal versus 78% with spending adjustment is more persuasive than advisor lectures. Frame as 'choices' rather than 'cuts.'
- Market Panic Response: Do not dismiss the client's anxiety. Acknowledge feelings before providing facts. The sequence matters: emotion first, logic second. 'I understand this feels very different—let me show you something that might help put this in perspective.' Historical return data, the cost of market-timing, and the distinction between 'temporary loss' and 'permanent loss of capital' are key tools.
- Irrational Decision Requests: When clients want to make decisions that are clearly contrary to their interests (sell all equities during a crash, buy individual speculative stocks), advisors face a dilemma between client autonomy and fiduciary responsibility. One approach: 'I absolutely can place that trade for you. Before I do, my job requires me to show you what the historical data says about this type of decision. Can we spend 10 minutes reviewing that? Then if you still want to proceed, I'll execute it immediately.'
- Capacity and Cognitive Decline Concerns: Identify trusted contact information when accounts are established. If advisor observes concerning cognitive changes, address gently but directly. Involve family members only with client's consent. Simplify portfolio and communication. Refer to elder law attorney for appropriate legal planning.

knowledge:ch22:s22.3-22-3-multigeneratio.heading: 22.3 Multigenerational Relationship Management
knowledge:ch22:s22.3-22-3-multigeneratio.content_summary: The 'Great Wealth Transfer' of $84 trillion over the next 20 years represents the largest wealth transition in history—and one of the greatest risks to advisor businesses. Research shows that 70% of adult children change financial advisors within a year of inheriting assets. Building relationships with clients' children and grandchildren is an essential retention strategy.

- Digital-First Engagement: Younger generations prefer mobile access, video meetings, and digital communication. Ensure technology platform meets their expectations.

knowledge:ch23:s23.1.2-key-planning-issu.heading: Key Planning Issues and Recommendations
knowledge:ch23:s23.1.2-key-planning-issu.content_summary:
- Pre-IPO 83(b) Election Window: If David has unvested RSAs (not RSUs), he should have filed an 83(b) election at grant to lock in low ordinary income and convert future appreciation to LTCG. RSUs do not allow 83(b) elections. Verify grant types.
- ISO Exercise Strategy Before IPO: Exercising ISOs (100,000 × $38 spread at exercise = $3.8M AMT preference item) pre-IPO while stock is still illiquid avoids creating public company AMT problem. Model AMT impact. If AMT exposure is manageable, exercis…
knowledge:ch23:s23.1.2-key-planning-issu.raw_text:
- Pre-IPO 83(b) Election Window: If David has unvested RSAs (not RSUs), he should have filed an 83(b) election at grant to lock in low ordinary income and convert future appreciation to LTCG. RSUs do not allow 83(b) elections. Verify grant types.
- ISO Exercise Strategy Before IPO: Exercising ISOs (100,000 × $38 spread at exercise = $3.8M AMT preference item) pre-IPO while stock is still illiquid avoids creating public company AMT problem. Model AMT impact. If AMT exposure is manageable, exercise all ISOs pre-IPO to start LTCG holding period and avoid ordinary income on exercise.
- Lock-Up Period Planning: Post-IPO, insiders typically face 180-day lock-up. Plan for diversification immediately upon lock-up expiration. Rule 10b5-1 plan (established in pre-IPO period during open window) enables systematic selling without insider trading concerns.
- RSU Tax Withholding Gap: RSUs vesting at IPO will be withheld at supplemental wage rate (22% federal) but effective marginal rate will be 37% + California/state taxes + NIIT. Model the withholding gap and plan for estimated tax payment at RSU vesting.
- Charitable Planning with IPO Stock: Pre-IPO stock donated to DAF (if allowed by company) or via Charitable Lead Trust can transfer appreciation outside taxable estate. Post-IPO, donating shares immediately after lock-up expiration is the most tax-efficient charitable giving method.
- College Funding: Superfund two 529 plans with $90,000 each ($180,000 total from David and Sarah's joint annual exclusion gift acceleration) as soon as liquid proceeds are available. FAFSA consideration: IPO year income is high; financial aid applications should be timed relative to 'base year' income.
- Estate Planning: Concentrated wealth at relatively young age with significant appreciation potential argues for: ILIT to hold life insurance (exclude from estate), SLAT (Spousal Lifetime Access Trust) to move assets outside estate while accessing them through spouse, annual gifting program to children's trusts.

knowledge:ch23:s23.2.2-key-planning-issu.raw_text:
- Business Valuation and Sale Preparation: Commission third-party valuation now (not at sale time) to understand realistic value and identify value drivers. Common HVAC company multiples: 4–6x EBITDA. At $1.5M EBITDA, potential range $6M–$9M. Value enhancement initiatives (recurring maintenance contracts, fleet management, technology investment, management depth) can increase multiple from 4x to 5–6x, adding $1.5–3M in value.
- Sale Structure Analysis: Asset sale vs. stock sale analysis critical for S-corp. Asset sale: buyer prefers (gets stepped-up basis); seller faces ordinary income on depreciation recapture plus capital gains on goodwill. Stock sale: seller prefers (all capital gains); buyer dislikes. Negotiation required—seller may need to offer price concession to buyer in exchange for stock sale treatment. Section 338(h)(10) election may be possible to give buyer asset-sale tax treatment while seller receives stock sale proceeds.
- ESOP Analysis: With 45 employees and $1.5M EBITDA, ESOP may be viable. C-corp conversion + ESOP sale: Robert could contribute non-recognition of capital gains (Section 1042 rollover) into Qualified Replacement Property (diversified portfolio of stocks and bonds in US operating companies). Significant planning and setup costs (~$150,000–$200,000) but potential tax savings of $1M+. Requires ESOP trustee; ongoing administration.
- Retirement Income Planning: Assess gap between investment income and $12,000/month target. Social Security: Robert's PIA at 67 = estimated $3,200/month (delay to 70 for $4,224/month). Patricia's PIA = estimated $2,400/month at 67. At 70: household SS = approximately $6,600/month. Gap: $5,400/month from portfolio investments. Portfolio withdrawal rate from $5–6M (after charitable giving) = 1–1.5%—very sustainable.
- Charitable Planning: Donate business stock (pre-sale) to Charitable Lead Annuity Trust (CLAT) or fund a DAF immediately upon closing for maximum income-year deduction. If $1.5M donated to hospital endowment in closing year, the charitable deduction significantly offsets the capital gains income spike.
- Estate Plan Update: With estate potentially exceeding $10M+ post-sale (over 2 adult children's shares), estate tax planning is relevant. Strategies: Gift business interests to FLP or LLC with valuation discount (15–25%) before sale for estate/gift tax purposes; GRAT to transfer appreciation to children; annual gifting program ($36,000/year per child per donor).

knowledge:ch23:s23.3.2-key-planning-issu.raw_text:
- Inherited IRA Rules: Critical compliance issue. Thomas passed at age 74 (past RBD of 72). Eleanor, as surviving spouse, has options: (1) Treat as own IRA—delay RMDs to her own RBD, roll into own IRA; (2) Treat as inherited IRA under 10-year rule. Optimal: Roll into Eleanor's own IRA (she's under 73 until next year). This delays RMDs based on her own life expectancy and provides more flexibility. Must be completed within 60 days of distribution or via direct trustee-to-trustee transfer.
- Step-Up in Basis: The inherited $3.2M portfolio received a step-up in basis to date-of-death values. Eleanor now owns these assets with essentially zero embedded gain. This is an exceptional opportunity: the portfolio can be restructured without capital gains consequences to align with her risk tolerance and income needs.
- Portfolio Restructuring: At age 72 with $4,500/month in guaranteed income (SS + pension), Eleanor's income gap is only $2,000/month ($24,000/year). Withdrawal rate from $4.5M portfolio = 0.5%—extremely sustainable. Portfolio can maintain significant equity exposure despite her age. Recommended allocation: 50–60% equity, 40–50% fixed income, with 18-month cash reserve.
- Cognitive Impairment Planning: Immediate priority—establish or confirm: Durable Power of Attorney (identify agent); Revocable Living Trust (avoid probate; trustee succession if Eleanor loses capacity; professional trustee or institutional trustee if children not nearby or capable); Healthcare Proxy; Simplified portfolio (fewer, simpler holdings; one custodian; clear beneficiary designations). Identify trusted contact. Consider professional co-trustee.
- Social Security Survivor Benefit: Verify Eleanor's current Social Security is the higher of her own benefit or Thomas's survivor benefit. If Thomas's benefit (which may have been higher after his lifetime of higher earnings) is larger, Eleanor may be entitled to switch to survivor benefit. Optimization analysis required.
- QCDs for Charitable Giving: Eleanor (70½+) can make Qualified Charitable Distributions directly from IRA to charity (up to $105,000/year). When she begins RMDs (at 73), QCDs will satisfy RMD requirement while excluding the distribution from taxable income—more valuable than a deduction because it reduces AGI directly, potentially reducing Medicare IRMAA and Social Security taxability.

knowledge:ch24:s24.1-investment-concepts.content_summary:

knowledge:ch24:s24.1-investment-concepts.raw_text:
Term: Alpha; Definition: Risk-adjusted excess return above a benchmark; the return attributable to manager skill rather than market exposure. Alpha of 1% means portfolio outperformed benchmark by 1% after adjusting for risk taken.
Term: Asset Allocation; Definition: The distribution of a portfolio across asset classes (stocks, bonds, real estate, alternatives, cash). Research suggests asset allocation explains 90%+ of portfolio return variability over time.
Term: Beta; Definition: A measure of a security's or portfolio's volatility relative to a benchmark. Beta of 1.0 means same volatility as benchmark; 0.5 means half as volatile; 1.5 means 50% more volatile.
Term: CAGR; Definition: Compound Annual Growth Rate—the rate at which an investment would have grown if it grew at the same rate every year. Accounts for compounding. Example: $100K growing to $200K in 7 years = 10.4% CAGR.
Term: Correlation; Definition: Statistical measure (-1 to +1) of how two assets move in relation to each other. Correlation of +1 = perfect positive correlation (move together); 0 = no relationship; -1 = perfect negative correlation (move opposite).
Term: Diversification; Definition: Spreading investments across multiple assets, asset classes, geographies, and sectors to reduce portfolio risk. Works because imperfectly correlated assets smooth overall portfolio volatility.
Term: Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA); Definition: Investing a fixed dollar amount at regular intervals regardless of price. Results in buying more shares when prices are low and fewer when high; reduces timing risk but not necessarily return.
Term: Duration; Definition: A bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes; measured in years. A duration of 7 means the bond price will decrease approximately 7% for every 1% increase in interest rates.
Term: Efficient Frontier; Definition: In Modern Portfolio Theory, the set of optimal portfolios that offer the highest expected return for a given level of risk, or lowest risk for a given expected return. Plotted as a curve on a risk-return graph.
Term: Factor Investing; Definition: Investment approach targeting specific drivers of return (factors) such as value, momentum, quality, low volatility, and size. Based on academic research showing these factors deliver risk-adjusted outperformance over time.
Term: Inflation Risk; Definition: The risk that rising prices will erode the purchasing power of investment returns. A 5% nominal return with 4% inflation yields only 1% real return.
Term: Liquidity; Definition: The ease and speed with which an asset can be converted to cash at or near its fair market value without significantly affecting the market price.
Term: Maximum Drawdown; Definition: The largest peak-to-trough decline in portfolio value over a specified period. A measure of downside risk that captures the worst case a long-term investor would have experienced.
Term: Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT); Definition: Framework developed by Harry Markowitz (1952) showing how rational investors use diversification to optimize expected return for a given level of risk. Foundation of mean-variance optimization.
Term: Rebalancing; Definition: Periodically adjusting portfolio weights back to target allocations as markets cause drift from original targets. Enforces buy-low-sell-high discipline and maintains intended risk profile.
Term: Sharpe Ratio; Definition: Risk-adjusted return metric: (Portfolio Return – Risk-Free Rate) / Portfolio Standard Deviation. Higher Sharpe ratio indicates better risk-adjusted performance. Sharpe > 1.0 generally considered good.
Term: Standard Deviation; Definition: Statistical measure of return variability around the mean; used as a proxy for investment risk. Higher standard deviation means wider range of potential outcomes (more volatile).
Term: Time-Weighted Return (TWR); Definition: Performance calculation that eliminates the effect of cash flows (deposits and withdrawals); appropriate for evaluating manager skill since manager doesn't control client cash flows.
Term: Money-Weighted Return (MWR/IRR); Definition: Performance calculation that accounts for timing and size of cash flows; reflects the actual investor experience. Appropriate for measuring client's personal investment outcome.
Term: Yield Curve; Definition: A graphical representation of yields on bonds of the same credit quality but different maturities. Normal curve slopes upward (long-term yields > short-term); inverted curve historically precedes recessions.

knowledge:ch24:s24.2-tax-planning-terms.raw_text:
Term: Adjusted Gross Income (AGI); Definition: Total gross income minus specific above-the-line deductions. AGI is the starting point for calculating various tax benefits and limitations. Many deductions and credits phase out at higher AGI levels.
Term: Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT); Definition: A parallel tax system that eliminates many regular tax deductions and applies a flat rate (26% or 28%) to alternative minimum taxable income. Designed to ensure high-income taxpayers pay minimum tax.
Term: Backdoor Roth IRA; Definition: Strategy for high-income earners above Roth income limits: make non-deductible traditional IRA contribution ($7,000 in 2024), then immediately convert to Roth IRA. Pro-rata rule may apply if other traditional IRA balances exist.
Term: Capital Gain; Definition: The profit from selling a capital asset for more than its adjusted basis. Short-term (held ≤ 1 year): taxed at ordinary income rates. Long-term (held > 1 year): taxed at preferential rates of 0%, 15%, or 20%.
Term: Cost Basis; Definition: The original value of an asset for tax purposes, typically the purchase price plus transaction costs. Capital gain = Proceeds – Adjusted Basis. Higher basis = lower taxable gain.
Term: Estate Tax; Definition: Federal tax imposed on the taxable estate of a deceased person. 2024 exemption: $13.61M per person ($27.22M for married couples). Rate: 40% above exemption. Scheduled to revert to ~$7M in 2026 absent Congressional action.
Term: Gift Tax; Definition: Federal tax on transfers of property during lifetime exceeding annual exclusion ($18,000 per recipient in 2024). Taxable gifts reduce lifetime estate/gift tax exemption. Unlimited marital deduction for transfers to US citizen spouses.
Term: Installment Sale; Definition: Sale of property where seller receives payments over multiple years. Gain is recognized proportionally as payments are received, spreading tax liability and potentially keeping seller in lower brackets.
Term: NIIT (Net Investment Income Tax); Definition: 3.8% surtax on net investment income (interest, dividends, capital gains, rents, royalties) for taxpayers with MAGI above $200K (single) or $250K (married filing jointly). Created by Affordable Care Act.
Term: Roth Conversion; Definition: Transferring funds from a traditional (pre-tax) IRA to a Roth (after-tax) IRA. Converted amount is included in taxable income; future growth and qualified withdrawals are tax-free.
Term: Step-Up in Basis; Definition: When an asset is inherited, its tax basis is 'stepped up' to the fair market value at the date of the decedent's death. This eliminates the built-in capital gains that accrued during the decedent's lifetime.
Term: Tax-Loss Harvesting (TLH); Definition: Selling securities at a loss to realize capital losses that offset capital gains and up to $3,000 of ordinary income annually. Harvested losses carried forward indefinitely. Must avoid wash-sale rule.
Term: Wash-Sale Rule; Definition: IRS rule that disallows a capital loss if the same or 'substantially identical' security is purchased 30 days before or after the sale. Disallowed loss is added to basis of replacement security.

knowledge:glossary:capital-gain.heading: Capital Gain
knowledge:glossary:capital-gain.content_summary: The profit from selling a capital asset for more than its adjusted basis. Short-term (held ≤ 1 year): taxed at ordinary income rates. Long-term (held > 1 year): taxed at preferential rates of 0%, 15%, or 20%.

knowledge:glossary:cost-basis.heading: Cost Basis
knowledge:glossary:cost-basis.content_summary: The original value of an asset for tax purposes, typically the purchase price plus transaction costs. Capital gain = Proceeds – Adjusted Basis. Higher basis = lower taxable gain.

knowledge:ch24:s24.3-estate-planning-ter.content_summary:
Term: Bypass Trust (Credit Shelter Trust); Definition: Irrevocable trust funded at first spouse's death with amount equal to estate tax exemption; assets bypass surviving spouse's estate, potentially doubling estate tax exemption. Less commonly used after portability introduction.
Term: Dynasty Trust; Definition: Long-term irrevocable trust designed to hold wealth for multiple generations, often perpetually in states that have abolished the Rule Against Perpetuities (South Dakota, Nevada, Delawa…
knowledge:ch24:s24.3-estate-planning-ter.raw_text:
Term: Bypass Trust (Credit Shelter Trust); Definition: Irrevocable trust funded at first spouse's death with amount equal to estate tax exemption; assets bypass surviving spouse's estate, potentially doubling estate tax exemption. Less commonly used after portability introduction.
Term: Dynasty Trust; Definition: Long-term irrevocable trust designed to hold wealth for multiple generations, often perpetually in states that have abolished the Rule Against Perpetuities (South Dakota, Nevada, Delaware). Distributes income and principal per trustee discretion.
Term: GRAT (Grantor Retained Annuity Trust); Definition: Irrevocable trust where grantor contributes assets and retains right to receive annuity for a term; appreciation above IRS hurdle rate (7520 rate) passes to remainder beneficiaries gift-tax free. Zero-out GRAT structure minimizes gift tax.
Term: IDGT (Intentional Defective Grantor Trust); Definition: Irrevocable trust designed to be 'defective' for income tax purposes (grantor pays income taxes) but complete for gift/estate tax purposes. Grantor's payment of trust's income tax is effectively an additional tax-free gift to beneficiaries.
Term: ILIT (Irrevocable Life Insurance Trust); Definition: Irrevocable trust that owns a life insurance policy on the grantor; insurance proceeds paid into trust at death are outside the taxable estate. Trustee uses proceeds to provide liquidity for estate taxes or bequest to beneficiaries.
Term: Per Stirpes; Definition: Legal term for distributing assets 'by branch' of the family tree. If a beneficiary predeceases the grantor, that beneficiary's share passes to their descendants proportionally.
Term: Portability; Definition: Allowance for surviving spouse to use deceased spouse's unused estate tax exemption (DSUEA). Election must be made on timely filed estate tax return (Form 706) within 9 months of death, extended 6 months.
Term: Probate; Definition: Court-supervised legal process of validating a will and distributing a deceased person's estate. Assets with designated beneficiaries (life insurance, retirement accounts) or joint ownership with survivorship rights bypass probate.
Term: Revocable Living Trust (RLT); Definition: Trust created during grantor's lifetime that can be modified or revoked. Does not provide asset protection or estate tax benefits while grantor is alive. Primary benefit: probate avoidance and seamless asset management if grantor becomes incapacitated.
Term: SLAT (Spousal Lifetime Access Trust); Definition: Irrevocable trust funded with the grantor's assets for the benefit of the grantor's spouse. Removes assets from grantor's estate while giving spouse access. Strategy to use current high exemption before potential 2026 reduction. Reciprocal trust risk requires different trust structures.
Term: Testamentary Trust; Definition: Trust created by a will that comes into existence only at the testator's death. Does not avoid probate (assets must pass through probate to reach trust) but allows controlled distributions to beneficiaries over time.

knowledge:ch24:s24.4-retirement-planning.heading: Retirement Planning Terms
knowledge:ch24:s24.4-retirement-planning.content_summary:
Term: Accumulation Phase; Definition: The period of an investor's life during which they are saving and investing to build wealth for retirement. Characterized by regular contributions and long time horizon.
Term: Decumulation Phase; Definition: The retirement period during which accumulated assets are systematically converted into income. Primary risks: sequence of returns, longevity, inflation, healthcare costs.
Term: Defined Benefit (DB) Plan; Definition: Employer-sponsored retirement plan th…
knowledge:ch24:s24.4-retirement-planning.raw_text:
Term: Accumulation Phase; Definition: The period of an investor's life during which they are saving and investing to build wealth for retirement. Characterized by regular contributions and long time horizon.
Term: Decumulation Phase; Definition: The retirement period during which accumulated assets are systematically converted into income. Primary risks: sequence of returns, longevity, inflation, healthcare costs.
Term: Defined Benefit (DB) Plan; Definition: Employer-sponsored retirement plan that promises a specified monthly benefit at retirement based on salary history and years of service. Employer bears investment risk. Increasingly replaced by defined contribution plans.
Term: Defined Contribution (DC) Plan; Definition: Retirement savings plan where contributions are defined but benefits are not guaranteed. Employee (and sometimes employer) contributes to individual accounts; investment risk borne by employee. Examples: 401(k), 403(b), 457.
Term: IRMAA (Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount); Definition: Additional premium charged to Medicare Parts B and D beneficiaries with MAGI above certain thresholds (currently >$103,000 single / >$206,000 joint). Based on income from 2 years prior.
Term: Primary Insurance Amount (PIA); Definition: The Social Security retirement benefit at full retirement age (FRA), calculated from the 35 highest-earning years adjusted for wage inflation. Basis for all Social Security benefit calculations.
Term: Required Minimum Distribution (RMD); Definition: Minimum amount that must be withdrawn annually from traditional IRAs, 401(k)s, and other pre-tax retirement accounts beginning at age 73 (post-SECURE 2.0). Calculated based on prior year-end balance divided by IRS life expectancy factor.
Term: Safe Withdrawal Rate; Definition: The percentage of a portfolio that can be withdrawn annually with high probability of not depleting the portfolio over a retirement period. The 4% rule (derived from Bengen 1994 research) is common starting point; modern research suggests 3.3–4% range depending on allocation and time horizon.
Term: SECURE Act 2.0; Definition: Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2022 legislation making major changes to retirement rules: raised RMD age to 73 (75 by 2033); increased catch-up contributions; added emergency withdrawals; Roth SIMPLE/SEP IRA allowance; student loan matching; 529-to-Roth rollovers.
Term: Sequence of Returns Risk; Definition: The risk that the timing of investment returns—particularly large early losses during distribution phase—permanently damages portfolio longevity, even if average returns are adequate over the full period.
Term: QLAC (Qualified Longevity Annuity Contract); Definition: Deferred income annuity purchased with IRA funds; income may be deferred to age 85; excluded from RMD calculations (up to lesser of $200,000 or 25% of account balance in 2024). Provides longevity insurance using tax-deferred funds.

knowledge:glossary:required-minimum-dist.heading: Required Minimum Distribution (RMD)
knowledge:glossary:required-minimum-dist.content_summary: Minimum amount that must be withdrawn annually from traditional IRAs, 401(k)s, and other pre-tax retirement accounts beginning at age 73 (post-SECURE 2.0). Calculated based on prior year-end balance divided by IRS life expectancy factor.

knowledge:glossary:safe-withdrawal-rate.heading: Safe Withdrawal Rate
knowledge:glossary:safe-withdrawal-rate.content_summary: The percentage of a portfolio that can be withdrawn annually with high probability of not depleting the portfolio over a retirement period. The 4% rule (derived from Bengen 1994 research) is common starting point; modern research suggests 3.3–4% range depending on allocation and time horizon.

knowledge:ch24:s24.5-insurance-and-risk-.raw_text:
Term: Annuity; Definition: Contract between policyholder and insurance company; policyholder makes lump sum or series of payments in exchange for guaranteed income payments (immediate or deferred). Used for longevity risk management.
Term: Any-Occupation Disability; Definition: Disability insurance definition requiring the insured to be unable to perform any occupation for which they are reasonably suited by education, training, or experience. More restrictive than own-occupation definition.
Term: Death Benefit; Definition: The amount paid to the beneficiary upon the death of the insured under a life insurance policy. May be level term, increasing, or decreasing depending on policy type.
Term: Elimination Period; Definition: The waiting period between when disability begins and when disability insurance benefits begin. Common periods: 90, 180 days. Longer elimination period = lower premium.
Term: Guaranteed Renewable; Definition: Provision in disability or health insurance policy that guarantees the insurer cannot cancel the policy as long as premiums are paid; however, rates can be increased on a class basis.
Term: Long-Term Care (LTC) Insurance; Definition: Insurance coverage for services (nursing home, assisted living, home care) that assist with activities of daily living (ADLs). Benefits triggered when insured cannot perform 2+ of 6 ADLs or suffers cognitive impairment.
Term: Non-Cancelable (Non-Can); Definition: Premium disability insurance provision meaning the insurer cannot cancel the policy, increase premiums, or change benefits as long as premiums are paid. Gold standard for DI coverage.
Term: Own-Occupation Disability; Definition: Disability insurance definition under which benefits are paid if the insured cannot perform the material duties of their specific occupation, even if they can work in another capacity. Most favorable definition for high-income professionals.
Term: Term Life Insurance; Definition: Life insurance providing coverage for a specified period (term). Pure death benefit; no cash value accumulation. Most cost-efficient way to obtain large death benefit. Common terms: 10, 20, 30 years.
Term: Universal Life (UL) Insurance; Definition: Permanent life insurance with flexible premiums and death benefit; separate premium and cost-of-insurance charges; cash value earns interest rate set by insurer. Greater flexibility than whole life but less predictability.
Term: Whole Life Insurance; Definition: Permanent life insurance with guaranteed level premiums, guaranteed death benefit, and guaranteed cash value growth. More expensive than term; used for permanent death benefit needs, estate planning, or guaranteed cash value accumulation.

knowledge:ch24:s24.6-regulatory-and-prof.content_summary:
Term: AUM (Assets Under Management); Definition: Total market value of financial assets that a financial institution or advisor manages on behalf of clients. Primary determinant of revenue for fee-based advisory practices charging a percentage of AUM.
Term: Broker-Dealer (BD); Definition: A firm (or individual) that buys and sells securities for its own account or on behalf of customers. Subject to FINRA supervision. Compensation typically via commissions. Must meet suitability standard (post-Re…
knowledge:ch24:s24.6-regulatory-and-prof.raw_text:
Term: AUM (Assets Under Management); Definition: Total market value of financial assets that a financial institution or advisor manages on behalf of clients. Primary determinant of revenue for fee-based advisory practices charging a percentage of AUM.
Term: Broker-Dealer (BD); Definition: A firm (or individual) that buys and sells securities for its own account or on behalf of customers. Subject to FINRA supervision. Compensation typically via commissions. Must meet suitability standard (post-Reg BI: enhanced suitability / best interest standard).
Term: CFP (Certified Financial Planner); Definition: Professional designation awarded by the CFP Board to financial planners meeting education (bachelor's degree + CFP curriculum), examination (170-question exam), experience (6,000 hours, or 4,000 hours apprenticeship), and ethics requirements.
Term: CFA (Chartered Financial Analyst); Definition: Professional credential awarded by CFA Institute; requires passing three progressively difficult exams covering investment analysis, portfolio management, and ethics; 4,000 hours of investment-related experience required.
Term: ERISA (Employee Retirement Income Security Act); Definition: 1974 federal law setting minimum standards for most voluntarily established retirement and health plans in private industry. Governs plan fiduciaries, funding requirements, vesting, and participant rights.
Term: Fiduciary; Definition: A person or organization legally and ethically required to act in the best interests of another party. Financial advisors acting as fiduciaries must prioritize client interests above their own; must avoid conflicts of interest or disclose and manage them.
Term: FINRA (Financial Industry Regulatory Authority); Definition: Self-regulatory organization (SRO) overseeing broker-dealers and their registered representatives in the US. Licenses, regulates, and enforces rules for broker-dealer industry. Operates BrokerCheck database for public background checks.
Term: Form ADV; Definition: SEC registration document filed by investment advisers. Part 1: basic background information filed with SEC. Part 2 (Brochure): narrative document describing services, fees, conflicts of interest, and disciplinary history; must be provided to clients.
Term: Investment Adviser (IA); Definition: Individual or firm that provides investment advice for compensation and is registered with the SEC (managing >$110M) or state securities regulators. Subject to Investment Advisers Act of 1940; must act as fiduciary.
Term: Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI); Definition: SEC rule effective June 2020 requiring broker-dealers to act in the best interest of retail customers when making investment recommendations. Higher standard than suitability; lower standard than full Investment Adviser Act fiduciary duty.
Term: RIA (Registered Investment Adviser); Definition: Investment advisory firm registered with SEC or state. Provides investment advice as primary business; charges fees for advice (AUM-based, flat, hourly, or performance-based). Regulated under Investment Advisers Act of 1940.
Term: Suitability Standard; Definition: Regulatory requirement (pre-Reg BI) for broker-dealers to recommend only securities 'suitable' for the customer based on their financial situation, investment objectives, and risk tolerance. Does not require 'best interest' recommendation.

knowledge:glossary:suitability-standard.content_summary: Regulatory requirement (pre-Reg BI) for broker-dealers to recommend only securities 'suitable' for the customer based on their financial situation, investment objectives, and risk tolerance. Does not require 'best interest' recommendation.

tool:ch1.heading: Chapter 1: Enterprise Technology Architecture & Core Infrastructure
tool:ch1.content_summary: Chapter 1: Enterprise Technology Architecture & Core Infrastructure
tool:ch1.raw_text: This chapter provides a complete map of Meridian Wealth Advisors' enterprise technology environment—every server, cloud service, network component, and foundational system on which all wealth management tools operate. Understanding this architecture is essential for troubleshooting, capacity planning, vendor negotiations, and regulatory examinations.
tool:ch1.label: Chapter 1: Enterprise Technology Architecture & Core Infrastructure

tool:ch1:s1.1-1-1-technology-architectur.heading: 1.1 Technology Architecture Overview
tool:ch1:s1.1-1-1-technology-architectur.content_summary: Meridian operates a hybrid cloud architecture combining on-premises infrastructure (for latency-sensitive trading and regulatory data retention) with multi-cloud services (AWS and Microsoft Azure) for scalability, disaster recovery, and modern SaaS application hosting. The architecture follows a defense-in-depth security model with network segmentation, zero-trust access controls, and continuous monitoring.

The architecture follows a defense-in-depth security model with network segmentation, zero-trust access controls, and continuous monitoring.

tool:ch1:s1.1.1-network-topology-and-seg.raw_text:
Network Zone: DMZ (Perimeter); VLAN / Subnet: VLAN 10 / 10.1.1.0/24; Purpose: Hosts public-facing services: client portal, API gateway, web servers; Security Controls: WAF (Cloudflare), IDS/IPS (Palo Alto), DDoS protection, TLS 1.3 termination; Connected Systems: Client Portal (React/Node.js), API Gateway (Kong), Load Balancers (F5); Access Level: Internet-facing; no direct internal access
Network Zone: Application Tier; VLAN / Subnet: VLAN 20 / 10.2.0.0/16; Purpose: Hosts core business applications: CRM, portfolio management, financial planning; Security Controls: Next-gen firewall rules, micro-segmentation (VMware NSX), application-layer filtering; Connected Systems: Salesforce FSC, Orion Connect, eMoney, Tamarac, compliance engines; Access Level: Internal users via VPN/SSO; DMZ via API only
Network Zone: Database Tier; VLAN / Subnet: VLAN 30 / 10.3.0.0/16; Purpose: All databases: SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch; Security Controls: Encrypted at rest (AES-256), TDE for SQL Server, network ACLs restrict to app tier only; Connected Systems: Client DB, Portfolio DB, Compliance DB, Document Store, Analytics DW; Access Level: Application tier only; no direct user access
Network Zone: Trading Zone; VLAN / Subnet: VLAN 40 / 10.4.0.0/24; Purpose: Order management, FIX protocol engines, custodian connectivity; Security Controls: Dedicated firewall rules, FIX session encryption, IP whitelisting for custodians; Connected Systems: OMS (Orion Trading), FIX engines, Schwab/Fidelity/Pershing gateways; Access Level: Trading desk only; segregated from general network
Network Zone: Management Zone; VLAN / Subnet: VLAN 50 / 10.5.0.0/24; Purpose: IT administration, monitoring, backup infrastructure; Security Controls: MFA required, PAM (CyberArk), session recording, jump servers only; Connected Systems: Nagios/Zabbix, Veeam backup, Active Directory, SCCM, SIEM (Splunk); Access Level: IT team only; audited access
Network Zone: Guest / IoT; VLAN / Subnet: VLAN 60 / 10.6.0.0/24; Purpose: Visitor Wi-Fi, conference room displays, smart building systems; Security Controls: Internet-only; no internal network access; captive portal authentication; Connected Systems: Guest Wi-Fi, Crestron A/V, environmental sensors; Access Level: Isolated; no access to any business systems
Network Zone: AWS VPC (us-east-1); VLAN / Subnet: VPC / 172.16.0.0/16; Purpose: Cloud-hosted applications, DR environment, analytics workloads; Security Controls: Security groups, NACLs, AWS WAF, GuardDuty, CloudTrail logging; Connected Systems: DR replicas, Redshift DW, SageMaker ML, Lambda functions, S3 storage; Access Level: Site-to-site VPN from on-prem; IAM role-based access
Network Zone: Azure Tenant; VLAN / Subnet: VNet / 172.17.0.0/16; Purpose: Microsoft 365, Azure AD, Teams, SharePoint, Intune MDM; Security Controls: Conditional Access, Azure Sentinel SIEM, DLP policies, Defender for Cloud; Connected Systems: Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, Power BI, Intune; Access Level: All employees via Azure AD SSO; conditional access policies

Server Name: MWAPROD-SIEM01; Role: Splunk Enterprise (SIEM, log aggregation, compliance reporting); OS / Platform: RHEL 9 / Splunk Enterprise 9.2; CPU / RAM: 32 vCPU / 128GB; Storage: 20TB spinning (hot/warm/cold tiers); Location: On-Prem DC2; Redundancy: Indexer cluster with search head cluster; Tier: Tier 2 — Important
Server Name: MWAPROD-BACKUP01; Role: Veeam Backup & Replication server; OS / Platform: Windows Server 2022 / Veeam 12; CPU / RAM: 16 vCPU / 64GB; Storage: 100TB (Quantum tape library + S3 cold); Location: On-Prem DC2; Redundancy: Off-site tape rotation + S3 Glacier Deep Archive; Tier: Tier 2 — Important
Server Name: MWADEV-ALL01–04; Role: Development / staging environment (all applications); OS / Platform: Mixed (mirrors production OS); CPU / RAM: 8 vCPU / 32GB each; Storage: 500GB SSD each; Location: AWS us-east-1; Redundancy: No redundancy (dev/test only); Tier: Tier 3 — Non-Critical

tool:ch1:s1.4-1-4-identity-access-manage.heading: 1.4 Identity & Access Management (IAM) Architecture
tool:ch1:s1.4-1-4-identity-access-manage.content_summary:
All user authentication flows through Azure Active Directory (Entra ID) as the primary identity provider, federated with on-premises Active Directory for legacy systems. Every application in the Meridian ecosystem is integrated via SAML 2.0 or OAuth 2.0/OIDC for single sign-on.
IAM Component: Primary IdP; Product: Azure AD (Entra ID) P2; Function: Central identity store; SSO; conditional access; MFA enforcement; Key Configuration: Passwordless preferred (FIDO2 keys + Microsoft Authenticator); le…
tool:ch1:s1.4-1-4-identity-access-manage.raw_text:
All user authentication flows through Azure Active Directory (Entra ID) as the primary identity provider, federated with on-premises Active Directory for legacy systems. Every application in the Meridian ecosystem is integrated via SAML 2.0 or OAuth 2.0/OIDC for single sign-on.
IAM Component: Primary IdP; Product: Azure AD (Entra ID) P2; Function: Central identity store; SSO; conditional access; MFA enforcement; Key Configuration: Passwordless preferred (FIDO2 keys + Microsoft Authenticator); legacy: TOTP MFA. Conditional access: require compliant device + MFA for all apps; block legacy auth protocols; Integration Points: All SaaS apps via SAML/OIDC; on-prem AD via Azure AD Connect sync
IAM Component: On-Prem Directory; Product: Active Directory (Windows Server 2022); Function: Legacy authentication for on-prem servers, file shares, printers; Key Configuration: Azure AD Connect with password hash sync + passthrough authentication; GPOs enforce password complexity (14+ chars, no expiry, breach detection); Integration Points: Azure AD sync; RADIUS for VPN; LDAP for legacy apps
IAM Component: Privileged Access Management; Product: CyberArk Privilege Cloud; Function: Vault for admin credentials; session recording; just-in-time access; Key Configuration: All admin accounts vaulted; 4-hour checkout maximum; dual approval for Tier 1 systems; full session recording for compliance; Integration Points: AD admin accounts, database SA accounts, cloud root/admin, network device credentials
IAM Component: Multi-Factor Authentication; Product: Microsoft Authenticator + YubiKey; Function: Second factor for all user authentication; phishing-resistant for admins; Key Configuration: Advisors: push notification MFA. IT admins: FIDO2 hardware key required. Clients (portal): SMS + email OTP (upgrading to passkeys Q3 2026); Integration Points: Azure AD conditional access; VPN gateway; CyberArk checkout; client portal
IAM Component: SSO Broker; Product: Azure AD Enterprise Apps; Function: SAML/OIDC federation hub for 45+ applications; Key Configuration: Each app has dedicated enterprise app registration; attribute mapping; group-based assignment; session lifetime 8 hours (12 hours for mobile); Integration Points: Salesforce, Orion, eMoney, Tamarac, Schwab Advisor Center, Fidelity WealthScape, DocuSign, Zoom, Smarsh, all internal apps
IAM Component: Identity Governance; Product: Azure AD Identity Governance; Function: Access reviews, entitlement management, lifecycle workflows; Key Configuration: Quarterly access reviews for all Tier 1 systems; automatic deprovisioning on termination (HR → AD → Azure AD → all apps within 1 hour); guest access expiry 90 days; Integration Points: HR system (BambooHR) triggers provisioning/deprovisioning; manager approval workflows
IAM Component: API Authentication; Product: OAuth 2.0 / API Keys; Function: Machine-to-machine authentication for integrations and data pipelines; Key Configuration: Service principals in Azure AD for cloud APIs; API keys rotated quarterly; rate limiting per client; JWT token validation at API gateway (Kong); Integration Points: Custodian APIs (Schwab, Fidelity, Pershing), market data feeds, internal microservices
Table 1.4: Identity & Access Management Architecture

tool:ch2.heading: Chapter 2: Client Relationship Management (CRM) Systems
tool:ch2.raw_text: The CRM is the operational heart of Meridian's advisory practice—the single source of truth for client data, the workflow engine for service delivery, and the compliance documentation system for regulatory examinations. This chapter documents every module, integration, data field, workflow, and administrative procedure for Meridian's CRM ecosystem.
tool:ch2.label: Chapter 2: Client Relationship Management (CRM) Systems

tool:ch2:s2.1-2-1-primary-crm-salesforce.heading: 2.1 Primary CRM: Salesforce Financial Services Cloud
tool:ch2:s2.1-2-1-primary-crm-salesforce.content_summary: Meridian migrated from Redtail CRM to Salesforce Financial Services Cloud (FSC) in Q2 2025, driven by the need for enterprise-grade workflow automation, deeper analytics, and superior integration capabilities with Orion, eMoney, and compliance tools. FSC provides a wealth-management-specific data model built on the Salesforce Lightning platform.

tool:ch2:s2.1.1-salesforce-fsc-data-mode.raw_text:
Object: Person Account; API Name: Account (PersonAccount); Purpose: Central client record combining contact and account; Key Fields: Name, SSN (encrypted), DOB, Address, Phone, Email, Risk Tolerance, AUM, Revenue, Client Since, Service Tier, Advisor Assignment; Relationships: 1-to-many: Financial Accounts, Opportunities, Activities, Documents, Household; Record Count (Current): 4,200 active clients; Data Sensitivity: PII — Restricted
Object: Household; API Name: FinServ__Household__c; Purpose: Groups related person accounts into economic unit; Key Fields: Household Name, Total AUM, Number of Members, Primary Contact, Service Tier Override, Annual Revenue; Relationships: 1-to-many: Person Accounts (members); 1-to-1: Financial Plan; Record Count (Current): 2,800 households; Data Sensitivity: Confidential
Object: Financial Account; API Name: FinServ__FinancialAccount__c; Purpose: Each custodial account, IRA, trust, 529, etc.; Key Fields: Account Number, Account Type (IRA, Roth, Joint, Trust, 529, etc.), Custodian, Current Value, Cost Basis, Inception Date, Benchmark, Model Portfolio, Tax Status; Relationships: Many-to-1: Person Account (owner); 1-to-many: Holdings, Transactions; Record Count (Current): 11,500 accounts; Data Sensitivity: Confidential — PII
Object: Financial Holding; API Name: FinServ__FinancialHolding__c; Purpose: Individual security positions within an account; Key Fields: Symbol, CUSIP, Shares, Market Value, Cost Basis, Unrealized Gain/Loss, Asset Class, Sector, Last Updated; Relationships: Many-to-1: Financial Account; Record Count (Current): 185,000+ holdings; Data Sensitivity: Confidential
Object: Opportunity; API Name: Opportunity; Purpose: Sales pipeline: prospective clients, asset transfers, rollovers; Key Fields: Stage (Lead, Qualified, Proposal, Won, Lost), Amount, Close Date, Source (Referral, COI, Web, Seminar), Advisor, Probability; Relationships: Many-to-1: Person Account; Record Count (Current): 350 active opportunities; Data Sensitivity: Internal
Object: Activity (Task/Event); API Name: Task / Event; Purpose: All client touchpoints: calls, meetings, emails, reviews; Key Fields: Subject, Date, Duration, Type (Call, Meeting, Email, Review), Notes, Compliance Approved, Related To; Relationships: Many-to-1: Person Account, Household, Opportunity; Record Count (Current): 45,000+ per year; Data Sensitivity: Confidential
Object: Financial Plan; API Name: Custom: MWA_Financial_Plan__c; Purpose: Links to eMoney/RightCapital plan; stores plan metadata; Key Fields: Plan Provider, Plan URL, Last Updated, Goal Achievement %, Monte Carlo Success Rate, Next Review Date; Relationships: Many-to-1: Household; 1-to-many: Goals; Record Count (Current): 2,200 active plans; Data Sensitivity: Confidential
Object: Case; API Name: Case; Purpose: Service requests: account changes, transfers, complaints; Key Fields: Case Number, Type (Transfer, Beneficiary Change, Address Update, Complaint, Fee Inquiry), Status, Priority, Resolution, SLA Due Date; Relationships: Many-to-1: Person Account; Record Count (Current): 3,500 per year; Data Sensitivity: Confidential — PII
Object: Document; API Name: ContentDocument / ContentVersion; Purpose: Attached files: statements, tax returns, signed forms; Key Fields: Title, File Type, Size, Upload Date, Category (Statement, Tax, Legal, Correspondence), Compliance Reviewed; Relationships: Many-to-many: Person Account, Financial Account, Case; Record Count (Current): 120,000+ documents; Data Sensitivity: Confidential — PII
Object: Referral; API Name: Custom: MWA_Referral__c; Purpose: Tracks referral source and outcome; Key Fields: Referrer (Person Account or COI), Referred Prospect, Date, Outcome, Revenue Generated, Thank You Sent; Relationships: Many-to-1: Person Account (referrer and prospect); Record Count (Current): 400 per year; Data Sensitivity: Internal

tool:ch2:s2.2-2-2-crm-workflow-automatio.heading: 2.2 CRM Workflow Automations
tool:ch2:s2.2-2-2-crm-workflow-automatio.content_summary:
Meridian has configured 35+ automated workflows in Salesforce to enforce service standards, compliance requirements, and operational efficiency. Below are the most critical automations.
Workflow Name: New Client Onboarding; Trigger: Opportunity Stage = 'Won'; Actions: Create Person Account → Create Financial Accounts → Generate DocuSign envelope (IPS + IMA + Privacy Notice) → Create onboarding Case → Assign to operations team → Schedule 30-day welcome call Task; Business Purpose: Ensure consiste…
tool:ch2:s2.2-2-2-crm-workflow-automatio.raw_text:
Meridian has configured 35+ automated workflows in Salesforce to enforce service standards, compliance requirements, and operational efficiency. Below are the most critical automations.
Workflow Name: New Client Onboarding; Trigger: Opportunity Stage = 'Won'; Actions: Create Person Account → Create Financial Accounts → Generate DocuSign envelope (IPS + IMA + Privacy Notice) → Create onboarding Case → Assign to operations team → Schedule 30-day welcome call Task; Business Purpose: Ensure consistent, compliant onboarding for every new client; no manual steps missed; Owner: Operations
Workflow Name: Quarterly Review Scheduler; Trigger: January 1, April 1, July 1, October 1 (scheduled); Actions: For each Platinum/Gold client: create Event for quarterly review → assign to primary advisor → send client email invitation (merge template) → create prep Task for associate; Business Purpose: Guarantee proactive client communication cadence per service tier; Owner: Client Service
Workflow Name: Birthday & Anniversary Alerts; Trigger: Daily batch: DOB or Client Since anniversary within 7 days; Actions: Create Task for advisor with client name, date, and suggested action (handwritten note, call, small gift per tier); Business Purpose: Personal touch that differentiates service; retention driver; Owner: Client Service
Workflow Name: AUM Change Alert; Trigger: Financial Account: AUM decreases >15% in 30 days (Orion feed); Actions: Create high-priority Task for advisor: 'Review significant AUM decline' with account details → escalate to team lead if not acted on within 48 hours; Business Purpose: Early warning for potential client dissatisfaction, market-driven anxiety, or unauthorized withdrawals; Owner: Compliance/Advisor
Workflow Name: Large Transfer Alert; Trigger: Financial Account: single transaction >$50,000 (incoming or outgoing); Actions: Create Compliance Case → notify CCO via email → create advisor Task → log for AML review; Business Purpose: AML/KYC compliance; elder financial exploitation detection; unusual activity monitoring; Owner: Compliance
Workflow Name: Complaint Tracking; Trigger: Case Type = 'Complaint' created; Actions: Assign to CCO → create regulatory tracking record → set SLA timer (24-hour acknowledgment, 30-day resolution) → generate FINRA complaint log entry; Business Purpose: SEC/FINRA complaint documentation requirements; regulatory examination readiness; Owner: CCO
Workflow Name: Fee Billing Reconciliation; Trigger: Monthly (1st business day); Actions: Pull Orion billing data → match to Salesforce Financial Accounts → flag discrepancies >$50 → create reconciliation Case → route to billing team; Business Purpose: Ensure accurate fee collection; identify billing errors before client notices; Owner: Finance
Workflow Name: Orphan Account Detection; Trigger: Weekly batch scan; Actions: Identify Financial Accounts with no primary advisor assigned or advisor = terminated employee → create Case → route to team lead for reassignment; Business Purpose: Prevent service gaps from advisor departures; ensure every account has responsible advisor; Owner: Operations
Workflow Name: Risk Tolerance Mismatch; Trigger: Nightly: compare Riskalyze score to portfolio actual risk (Orion); Actions: If portfolio risk score deviates >20% from stated tolerance → create compliance Task → notify advisor → document for suitability records; Business Purpose: Ongoing suitability monitoring; SEC/FINRA best interest documentation; Owner: Compliance
Workflow Name: Document Expiration Tracker; Trigger: Weekly: scan documents for expiration dates; Actions: Flag expired: driver's licenses (KYC), trust documents >5 years old, insurance policies, estate plans >3 years → create Task for advisor to request updated copies; Business Purpose: Maintain current KYC/AML documentation; ensure estate plans reflect current law and wishes; Owner: Compliance
Table 2.2: Critical CRM Workflow Automations

tool:ch2:s2.3-2-3-crm-integration-map.heading: 2.3 CRM Integration Map
tool:ch2:s2.3-2-3-crm-integration-map.content_summary:
Salesforce FSC is the central hub connecting to 15+ external systems. Each integration follows a standardized pattern: real-time where latency matters, batch/scheduled where volume efficiency matters.
Source System: Orion Connect (Portfolio); Direction: Orion → Salesforce; Integration Method: REST API (Orion API v2) → Salesforce Platform Events; Data Exchanged: Account values, holdings, performance, billing, transactions; Frequency: Real-time for AUM updates; nightly batch for full reconciliatio…
tool:ch2:s2.3-2-3-crm-integration-map.raw_text:
Salesforce FSC is the central hub connecting to 15+ external systems. Each integration follows a standardized pattern: real-time where latency matters, batch/scheduled where volume efficiency matters.
Source System: Orion Connect (Portfolio); Direction: Orion → Salesforce; Integration Method: REST API (Orion API v2) → Salesforce Platform Events; Data Exchanged: Account values, holdings, performance, billing, transactions; Frequency: Real-time for AUM updates; nightly batch for full reconciliation; Error Handling: Dead letter queue in AWS SQS; retry 3x with exponential backoff; alert to IT; Monitoring: CloudWatch dashboard; Slack #integrations channel alerts
Source System: eMoney Advisor; Direction: Bidirectional; Integration Method: eMoney API ↔ Salesforce REST; Data Exchanged: Client demographics, plan links, goal data, net worth; Frequency: Nightly sync (demographics); on-demand (plan links); Error Handling: Log to Splunk; manual reconciliation weekly; Monitoring: Splunk dashboard; weekly reconciliation report
Source System: DocuSign; Direction: DocuSign → Salesforce; Integration Method: DocuSign Connect (webhook); Data Exchanged: Signed document status, completed envelopes, audit trail; Frequency: Real-time (event-driven on signature completion); Error Handling: Webhook retry (72 hours); manual re-pull if failed; Monitoring: DocuSign admin console; Salesforce integration logs
Source System: Schwab Advisor Services; Direction: Bidirectional; Integration Method: Schwab API (SFTP for bulk; REST for real-time); Data Exchanged: Account data, money movement, ACATS transfers, cost basis; Frequency: SFTP: nightly. REST: real-time for new accounts; Error Handling: SFTP file monitoring; email alert on missing files; Monitoring: Custom Splunk dashboard
Source System: Fidelity Institutional; Direction: Bidirectional; Integration Method: Fidelity Integration Xchange (FIX) + SFTP; Data Exchanged: Account data, positions, transactions, cost basis, tax lots; Frequency: SFTP: nightly. FIX: real-time trade confirmations; Error Handling: FIX session monitoring; SFTP file validation; Monitoring: FIX engine log monitoring; file receipt alerts
Source System: Riskalyze (Nitrogen); Direction: Riskalyze → Salesforce; Integration Method: REST API; Data Exchanged: Risk scores, questionnaire results, portfolio risk analysis; Frequency: On-demand (when questionnaire completed); nightly batch; Error Handling: API error logging; manual fallback; Monitoring: Salesforce integration log
Source System: Smarsh (Email Archive); Direction: Salesforce → Smarsh; Integration Method: SMTP relay + API; Data Exchanged: Email metadata for compliance linking; archived email references; Frequency: Real-time (email capture); daily batch (metadata sync); Error Handling: Smarsh connector retry; CCO notification; Monitoring: Smarsh admin dashboard
Source System: BambooHR; Direction: BambooHR → Salesforce; Integration Method: REST API via MuleSoft; Data Exchanged: Employee data: new hires, terminations, role changes → trigger user provisioning/deprovisioning; Frequency: Real-time (event-driven) + daily reconciliation; Error Handling: MuleSoft error queue; HR notification; Monitoring: MuleSoft Anypoint monitoring
Source System: Morningstar Direct; Direction: Morningstar → Salesforce (indirect); Integration Method: File export → S3 → Lambda → Salesforce; Data Exchanged: Fund research data, model portfolio holdings, performance attribution; Frequency: Weekly (Saturday overnight); Error Handling: Lambda error → SNS alert → IT; Monitoring: CloudWatch; S3 event notifications
Source System: Client Portal (Custom); Direction: Bidirectional; Integration Method: Salesforce REST API (Experience Cloud); Data Exchanged: Client profile, document requests, secure messaging, meeting scheduling; Frequency: Real-time; Error Handling: Circuit breaker pattern; graceful degradation to cached data; Monitoring: New Relic APM; Salesforce API usage dashboard
